title: Ἀλώπηξ καὶ πίθηκος ⟨βασιλεὺς αἱρεθείς⟩
titleEn: The Fox and the Monkey Made King
part: The Fox and the Monkey Made King (Chambry 38 · Perry 81)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 38 (= Perry 81). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἐν συνόδῳ τῶν ἀλόγων ζῴων πίθηκος ὀρχησάμενος καὶ εὐδοκιμήσας βασιλεὺς ὑπ’ αὐτῶν ἐχειροτονήθη.
sentences.tr: En synodōi tōn alogōn zōiōn pithēkos orchēsamenos kai eudokimēsas basileus hyp’ autōn echeirotonēthē.
sentences.l: In an assembly of the speechless animals a monkey, having danced and having won approval, was elected king by them.
sentences.i: At an assembly of the beasts a monkey danced, was well thought of, and was voted king by them.
sentences.n: τὰ ἄλογα ζῷα, “the animals without λόγος” — without speech and without reason — is the standard Greek term for beasts, and quietly funny in a fable where they hold a vote. ἐχειροτονήθη is the Athenian technical verb for electing by show of hands (χείρ, “hand”): the animals meet in σύνοδος and vote as citizens do.

sentences.t: Ἀλώπηξ δὲ αὐτῷ φθονήσασα, ὡς ἐθεάσατο ἔν τινι πάγῃ κρέας κείμενον, ἀγαγοῦσα αὐτὸν ἐνταῦθα ἔλεγεν ὡς εὑροῦσα θησαυρὸν αὐτὴ μὲν οὐκ ἐχρήσατο, γέρας δὲ αὐτῷ τῆς βασιλείας τετήρηκε, καὶ παρῄνει αὐτῷ λαμβάνειν.
sentences.tr: Alōpēx de autōi phthonēsasa, hōs etheasato en tini pagēi kreas keimenon, agagousa auton entautha elegen hōs heurousa thēsauron autē men ouk echrēsato, geras de autōi tēs basileias tetērēke, kai parēinei autōi lambanein.
sentences.l: And a fox, having envied him, when she beheld meat lying in a certain trap, having led him there, said that she, having found a treasure, had not used it herself, but had kept it for him as a prize of the kingship, and she urged him to take it.
sentences.i: A fox, who envied him, caught sight of a piece of meat lying in a trap; she brought him to the spot and told him she had found a treasure and had not made use of it herself, but had kept it for him as the perquisite of his kingship, and she pressed him to take it.
sentences.n: φθονεῖν takes the dative of the person envied (αὐτῷ). ὡς after ἔλεγεν introduces reported speech, and Greek keeps the tenses the fox herself used (ἐχρήσατο, τετήρηκε) instead of shifting them back as English does. γέρας is the portion of honour set aside for a king or a chief — a Homeric word, and flattery in her mouth.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ ἀτημελήτως ἐπελθόντος καὶ ὑπὸ τῆς πάγης συλληφθέντος, αἰτιωμένου τε τὴν ἀλώπεκα ὡς ἐνεδρεύσασαν αὐτῷ, ἐκείνη ἔφη· « Ὦ πίθηκε, σὺ δὲ τοιαύτην μωρίαν ἔχων τῶν ἀλόγων ζῴων βασιλεύεις ; »
sentences.tr: Tou de atēmelētōs epelthontos kai hypo tēs pagēs syllēphthentos, aitiōmenou te tēn alōpeka hōs enedreusasan autōi, ekeinē ephē· « Ō pithēke, sy de toiautēn mōrian echōn tōn alogōn zōiōn basileueis ; »
sentences.l: And he having come up heedlessly and having been caught by the trap, and blaming the fox as having ambushed him, she said: « Monkey, and you, having such folly as this, are king over the speechless animals? »
sentences.i: He went up carelessly and was caught in the trap; and when he reproached the fox for having laid a snare for him, she said, “Monkey — with folly like this in you, are you king over the beasts?”
sentences.n: One genitive absolute carrying three participles in a row (τοῦ … ἐπελθόντος, συλληφθέντος, αἰτιωμένου) holds the whole disaster suspended until the fox's reply lands. ὡς with the participle (ὡς ἐνεδρεύσασαν) gives the charge as the monkey makes it rather than as a fact: “on the ground that she had ambushed him.” βασιλεύειν takes the genitive of what one rules. Chambry's question mark is the Greek one, printed as “;” with a space before it.

sentences.t: Οὕτως οἱ τοῖς πράγμασιν ἀπερισκέπτως ἐπιχειροῦντες ἐπὶ τῷ δυστυχεῖν καὶ γέλωτα ὀφλισκάνουσιν.
sentences.tr: Houtōs hoi tois pragmasin aperiskeptōs epicheirountes epi tōi dystychein kai gelōta ophliskanousin.
sentences.l: So those who set their hands to affairs without looking about them, on top of faring badly, incur laughter as well.
sentences.i: So those who take a thing in hand without looking ahead not only come to grief, but are laughed at besides.
sentences.n: γέλωτα ὀφλισκάνειν is a fixed idiom: ὀφλισκάνω is the court word for losing a case and so incurring the penalty, and here the penalty is being laughed at. ἐπὶ τῷ δυστυχεῖν is an articular infinitive after ἐπί — “on top of the faring-badly.”
